Donald Trump has no intention of honoring free and fair election results post-November 3, 2026.
| | | | | [](https://yfq78zhbb.cc.rs6.net/tn.jsp?f=001Pp8v_RBIDQTB976-dvOHpaRQqpwOR7AOZR1DwXHWM7BhhUi0eBPP9ziD3xDDc8kpsTAiNXV8PIrwgZ7AJjPtJGCUMGqXm47ZYL91Ib92BShQ9bYorY-PmThbZn6ao7MUIKaXTnTLh9DB4EpSzFbj3-8uSnDUZRtgp5moSgyjBlEay2wydMqzJxG065y1ieyFAJ4s-jatK3f3uENeAoCPnr2RL7St1RhVdTEezXonJLM=&c=BZG1LlUaTkjHSVah7PEI6gHGYIXcrnECFUPlwGYu_EXS-jkSVsacMA==&ch=kF8kk7HKQn3o655vo4xp7k4RuSkK4__tj_d7l72aasrKqRyZoOaWLA==)

|
Peter,
Trump's weaponized DOJ is rolling out its first major intervention in the midterm election two weeks out from Election Day in California, attempting to invalidate ~20,000 alleged "noncitizen" voters.
First, the facts: DOJ is asking federal judges to halt the counting of thousands of ballots until voters' citizenship can be verified. This is a fishing expedition at best, and at worst an obvious attempt to gain a foothold toward declaring all of CA's elections "invalid" and cancelling even more ballots.
An LA County election official said that a sample of the 20k records at issue showed most of the people identified already had cancelled registrations; and of the others, a small number were mailed ballots (implying they were valid voters). Most of them had never voted.
Next, the truth: This is not about rooting out invalid or illegal voters. DOJ is already able to investigate and prosecute any fraudulent voting or noncitizen voters. States routinely cooperate with legal requests on specific cases.
It is about using the power and might of the federal government's top law enforcement agency to intimidate election officials, erode public trust in elections, and add another note to the fictional narrative Trump has created that fraudulent voting is widespread--even though no one can prove it.

One of the most remarkable shifts in U.S. politics since the 2024 elections--coincident with the rise of AI--is the emergence of a hardened, overwhelming, and bipartisan aversion to data centers.
We're currently in the "endlessly inundated with ads" phase of the '26 midterm elections, and everyone seems to be leaning into the attack that their opponent is pro-data center. [Republicans are using it to attack Democrats](https://substack.com/redirect/74a681b9-2812-4577-bb65-786f377f74e4?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg); [Democrats are using it to attack Republicans](https://substack.com/redirect/6a305c61-808f-4c2a-a3fb-b76069305371?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), [sometimes in the same race](https://substack.com/redirect/8e791651-83c3-4e26-8452-26dd9458419c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg);1 [ballot measure campaigns are using the tactic](https://substack.com/redirect/31140f36-1416-4850-aebf-1071ffea2eba?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) to win over voters even when their campaign has literally nothing to do with data centers.2
[Within a matter of months](https://substack.com/redirect/72402789-078f-4bac-a441-a28c0c5a03fd?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), support for building data centers has crumbled.
At the same time, setting aside the narrative, what I haven't seen: what's the real story with data centers? Where is public opinion on the mark, and where is public anger unjustified?3
I'm splitting this discussion across two articles. In this one, I'll talk about public opinion, what's driving those opinions, and the top reason Americans are concerned about data centers: their water use.
> _**Article summary:**_
> * _The water that data centers use is a minuscule percentage of the country 's total water use: less than 1%, even broadly defined. But that undersells the impact they're having._
> * _During the summer, in arid places, and in places without adequate regulation, the water data centers are using is a legitimate and growing problem._
> * _States and municipalities must update their laws to require more efficient technology and to charge more for data centers to use and consume water._
>

[ Subscribed](https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9iZW5zYW11ZWxzLnN1YnN0YWNrLmNvbS9hY2NvdW50IiwicCI6MjIwMjQzNTk3LCJzIjoyNDQwMzk4LCJmIjp0cnVlLCJ1Ijo5MDUwMTE5MiwiaWF0IjoxNzkyNTkxMDE2LCJleHAiOjIxMDgxNjcwMTYsImlzcyI6InB1Yi0wIiwic3ViIjoibGluay1yZWRpcmVjdCJ9.wVincWlrU2VNsXPcUoC9PblG1a_2Wojvc2444ng-Kzs?)
## Americans are concerned about data centers
Ordinarily, I'm perfectly comfortable using polling data from a year or two ago--certainly, from a few months ago--because while public opinion shifts on issues, it's usually pretty slow.
That's not the case with data centers. In a matter of months, public opinion on data centers has become [considerably more negative](https://substack.com/redirect/72402789-078f-4bac-a441-a28c0c5a03fd?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)--a change across every demographic and across both Republicans and Democrats.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/464b52d9-fccf-4d07-93df-cadd6cbecaa9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Source: [Ipsos](https://substack.com/redirect/60164793-ddc3-4653-b3d1-d15207a43884?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), September 9-10
For context, that's [higher than the percentage of Americans who are concerned](https://substack.com/redirect/5f84bdea-28a9-456b-a577-39471e788c15?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) about future terrorist attacks, crime, and unemployment.4 This is a real concern for people.
In the same poll, people who were concerned about the growth of data centers were asked why specifically they were concerned:
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/d6279c51-c92f-4f03-b48b-b5e6ba631a05?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Source: [Ipsos](https://substack.com/redirect/60164793-ddc3-4653-b3d1-d15207a43884?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), September 9-10
I'll use this data as a way of defining people's top six concerns with data centers.5 With data centers having become such a toxic political issue, I wanted to understand: **how real are these issues?** Where's the narrative about data centers right, and where is it wrong?
In this article, I'm focusing just on the top concern that Americans have: how much water data centers use. In the next one, I'll focus on the next five issues that worry us.

## 1\. Are data centers a strain on local water supplies?
Right now, the water that data centers use is a really, really small percentage of total water use in the United States. Data centers use about [38.5 billion gallons of water](https://substack.com/redirect/d18d66a7-f6d6-4949-b984-ee78392b3640?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) per year. The country as a whole uses [102.6 ](https://substack.com/redirect/3eb3b64b-5377-4440-9a51-5ba85cab67c1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_[trillion](https://substack.com/redirect/3eb3b64b-5377-4440-9a51-5ba85cab67c1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_ --that's 102,600 billion--gallons of freshwater per year.6 **Data centers make up about 0.04% of the country 's total water use.**
On the one hand, that's nothing.7 On the other, it almost certainly undersells how much water data centers consume, and undersells the impact that data centers have on water supplies in the U.S.
Even still, for most of the United States, we're a long way from water use becoming a substantial strain on our systems. But there are places where it is a real issue.
#### Water use ≠ water withdrawals ≠ water consumption
Before we dig into any of the data, there are some definitions that matter.
Water use is any water that we use: for households, for agriculture, for power, etc. Water withdrawals refer to any water removed from rivers, lakes, groundwater, etc. And water consumption is any water that isn't returned to the immediate water environment, usually because it's lost to evaporation or because it's incorporated into products.8
I give you (and myself) this lesson in ecology because how much water is _used_ generally matters less than how much water is _consumed_. It turns out that data centers are quite consumptive:
* [According to Google disclosures](https://substack.com/redirect/20d8f653-940e-43f0-a8fd-46c7bf8cd481?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), 78% of the water they use at their data centers is consumed.
* [According to Meta disclosures](https://substack.com/redirect/453bdcc3-f8d3-496c-984d-db51393faef5?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), 72% of the water they use at their data centers is consumed.

This is very high! It's on par with irrigation, where [72% of water use is consumptive](https://substack.com/redirect/5dd8f139-a319-4eed-b15f-df786b0d7eb7?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). There are two points I'd add here for important context.
First, [tech](https://substack.com/redirect/0a3f5dd8-1c63-4b08-b9fb-3aa10c72b912?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) [companies](https://substack.com/redirect/4ad9716e-d462-4adc-856e-77c4e7f741dc?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) [are](https://substack.com/redirect/a19b9a45-bb51-4de6-a896-194c525bb5d3?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) [promising](https://substack.com/redirect/9a8fb654-d6c6-419b-92b8-2edba9cb11bd?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) more efficient water use at their data centers, and while they have some incentive to overpromise here, their incentives are generally aligned--saving water generally saves money--and I suspect this technology will get better over time.
Second, while the data centers themselves may be highly consumptive, power production generally isn't. For power production, [only about 4% of water use](https://substack.com/redirect/afe0a178-d0df-4b0a-b178-a1f08169bbbf?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) is consumptive, though that varies considerably based on the mode of power generation.9
#### That 0.04% estimate doesn't include power generation
With that said, we should talk about the water that's being used to generate the power that runs data centers.
Saying that data centers account for 0.04% of the country's water use accounts only for direct water use, i.e., water used by the equipment on-site at data centers. But that discounts the water consumed by having to generate more energy--and [that indirect water consumption is estimated to be as much as 12× more](https://substack.com/redirect/98f99181-0869-4a0e-9129-5352c191d15a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) than any direct water consumption.10
Again, this varies a lot based on how the energy is being generated. But incremental power generation substantially increases the impact on water systems that data centers can have.
#### Water use is highly seasonal
[Water use is not constant](https://substack.com/redirect/a49f9baa-cfdd-4daf-bb3b-a0573e090910?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) throughout the year. Namely, in most of the United States, [water use is higher](https://substack.com/redirect/d11ed264-3537-4947-ae78-5361e60bf4a8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) during the summer.11
That's true at data centers too. Because it's warmer and [more water is needed for cooling](https://substack.com/redirect/0d02d196-c2cb-4c26-8db8-0fe61419c257?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), monthly water use at data centers is often [much higher during the summer than the rest of the year](https://substack.com/redirect/16baec17-3599-4b27-9658-686c0023acc9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). That coincides with periods--namely, the late summer and early fall--when American water levels are [generally at their lowest](https://substack.com/redirect/0d37998b-5333-4638-8864-163b7bfbdaab?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
So even if data centers use a low percentage of a region's water on average, they can still seasonally strain water systems because of when their water usage is highest.
#### Water usage varies greatly across the United States
Something else we all know: the [amount of water available](https://substack.com/redirect/deeb8b48-bb9a-4389-b8cb-7b3b81821224?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)--and the [amount of water used](https://substack.com/redirect/7da27bdb-9a81-4f81-94d5-6dca23296796?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)--varies drastically by state. Arizona, for instance, has the [seventh-most data centers](https://substack.com/redirect/6d01e28c-f832-4428-8fd3-7171b2ed23e6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) in the United States, at a time when its water availability is already under incredible strain because of a [sustained drought impacting the Colorado River](https://substack.com/redirect/5830b425-b2d7-49c4-9bd7-230e907076f8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
In [Arizona and elsewhere in the Mountain West](https://substack.com/redirect/836e1608-40bd-445f-8c1e-94d267dab58b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), where this is an issue, data centers are a particular threat. That's less true in other places where water availability is less of a pressing issue.
#### Left unregulated, data centers really can wreak havoc on local water
Back in 2006, Google opened a data center in [The Dalles, Oregon](https://substack.com/redirect/9f98607b-0838-4e06-8f10-dab5fe4b0803?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), a city with 16,000 people about 90 minutes east of Portland. Google has since opened several more there, and its [data centers use about 33% of the city's water supply](https://substack.com/redirect/d0bb545a-1d27-491e-b31a-8dab452cdf87?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).12
This creates all sorts of issues for the city (and for wildlife in the region).
In Louisiana, [Meta is building a data center](https://substack.com/redirect/195a54e3-3556-4b30-9acc-a6a677fbd8b6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) in [Richland Parish](https://substack.com/redirect/0a3fb7c0-2e58-4589-a4ac-a43fb56a9573?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).13 When it opens in 2028, its daily water usage is projected to be comparable to the [daily water usage for 17,000 people](https://substack.com/redirect/9a81bbd3-2c83-4298-8e2d-5a8bbdc7d6e3?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) in the parish, which is notable because only 20,000 people live there.14
There are plenty of examples like this from across America.
#### What's incorrect about the narrative about water use at data centers?
I already talked about the big thing: today, data centers are still using a tiny percentage of American water. For most of the country, it'd be wrong to say that this is a pressing, imminent threat.
If we were serious about addressing water use in the United States, [we'd start with agriculture](https://substack.com/redirect/45d5fd1f-6056-4455-980a-348a204a1e5d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), not data centers. [Agriculture is pretty horribly inefficient](https://substack.com/redirect/e7339b6f-d695-434c-a635-d00f214d287f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) and consumes substantially more water than data centers will anytime soon.
Yes, agriculture is also more essential. But small reductions in agricultural water consumption would outweigh even substantial improvements in the efficiency of water use at data centers.
But that doesn't mean that data centers shouldn't be doing much more--especially since they're poised to continue expanding at such a rapid pace.
**Verdict: the water that data centers use is a tiny percentage of America 's total water use. Data centers don't necessarily threaten the water supply in all of America, since they're so localized. But if you live in an area with data centers, or if you live in an arid area, they can--and do--have a real and lasting impact on water systems.**

## Regulating water use at data centers
Addressing water use is, famously, rather difficult to do. First of all, people--rightly--[get anxious](https://substack.com/redirect/b1abbc7c-32f9-4991-897a-a1b2d6981675?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) when anyone talks about increasing the rates for water use. But there are also very arcane rules that govern water use in much of the country, often a complicated weave of [property rights](https://substack.com/redirect/2cbfcde8-023f-40af-946a-f599d1fc9705?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) and [tribal sovereignty](https://substack.com/redirect/a948dc58-f2cd-4703-bb4b-8c751ba353f7?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) and [other long-standing agreements](https://substack.com/redirect/6c7aea58-05d1-440d-8783-8eabceaabc02?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) that make reforms challenging.
But since data centers are important--more on that in a moment--something here will have to give. There are a few policy proposals that states are trying to address water use and water consumption from data centers:
* [Oklahoma](https://substack.com/redirect/d5c95e12-4cae-4383-ac31-76a5b2ec20ea?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) bans the use of groundwater for cooling systems in data centers without recirculating the water.
* [Florida](https://substack.com/redirect/d5c95e12-4cae-4383-ac31-76a5b2ec20ea?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) requires its data centers to use reclaimed water in some situations, rather than drawing water directly from the environment.
* [California](https://substack.com/redirect/d5c95e12-4cae-4383-ac31-76a5b2ec20ea?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) will require data center applicants to estimate their water use and outline their plans in the event of water scarcity or drought.

But the biggest change will have to come from the data centers themselves, which will have to find ways to use less water, to reduce their water consumption rate, or both. And that is likely only possible if the cost of water at data centers goes up substantially.
States and municipalities should charge data centers much more to use their water. That will create a financial incentive for tech companies to invest in better, more efficient systems that both use and consume less water.15
Local governments should also enter into agreements that give them more flexibility to allocate and reallocate water rights to data centers as necessary.
## Chinese misinformation campaigns are part of the story here too
One thing that's lost in the debate about data centers: [they ](https://substack.com/redirect/2023dec3-badd-4ebe-9270-41e4e42fe439?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_[are](https://substack.com/redirect/2023dec3-badd-4ebe-9270-41e4e42fe439?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_[ important](https://substack.com/redirect/2023dec3-badd-4ebe-9270-41e4e42fe439?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). They're the engine for AI development, and AI is already an enormously important part of our economy. Does AI need to be properly regulated? Absolutely. But it's here to stay, and if America cares about global competitiveness, we have to invest in AI.
I bring this up because China is intent on reducing American public support for data center construction. If America slows down its data center development, that creates a competitive advantage for China.
[Donald Trump](https://substack.com/redirect/50b0dd8b-12ec-4274-b9fd-13b0df23be3c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) and Interior Secretary [Doug Burgum](https://substack.com/redirect/afebff47-a040-4235-928e-6de7da50735a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), among lots of others, have spoken about this. I'm generally not inclined to believe either of them, but in this case, [they're right](https://substack.com/redirect/a35eaac8-6abc-4d67-972e-d5c1b5543134?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). China [and other American adversaries](https://substack.com/redirect/fcba77aa-7574-46da-90be-bef654e38a7e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) are fanning the flames.
We have to be responsible in the way that we're building out data centers. But stopping them entirely is probably a mistake, and we should be aware that active campaigns are trying to drive more forceful public opposition.

Also: there's a report [from the Congressional Research Service](https://substack.com/redirect/9b875482-4dc4-4a03-a5ad-86f3dc0993c5?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) that says the following (emphasis added):
> Concerns over the water used by data centers have garnered congressional attention. **Data centers'**_**direct**_**water use** (i.e., water used or consumed at the data center for thermal regulation, not _indirect_ use of water used for off-site power generation or further up the supply chain for manufacturing computer hardware or building materials) **is estimated to make up a relatively small proportion (approximately 2%) of total U.S. water consumption.**
Best I can tell, this is totally wrong. That figure seems to come from an [American Water Works Association study](https://substack.com/redirect/7daa1359-efc5-4aca-a399-65deff27a97f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) which says the following (emphasis added):
> The 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report demonstrates this trend, with estimates reflecting that in 2014, 64% of direct water consumption came from internal data centers (i.e., data centers run by enterprises for their own internal use). By 2023, hyperscale and colocation (i.e., data centers built to serve multiple companies) were expected to account for 84% of total direct water consumption, with internal data centers accounting for just 12%. **This trend will likely to continue [sic] into 2028, with direct water consumption by internal data centers estimated at just 2% and hyperscale data centers increasing their consumption up to nearly 50% (33 billion gallons) of the total**.
The 2% figure here is referring to something much narrower and more technical: the share of direct data center water consumption projected to come from internal data centers in 2028. This doesn't say anything about the percentage of U.S. water consumption that comes from data centers.
I'm going to reach out once this is published to see if I can get that figure corrected in the CRS report.
7
Irrigation, which [includes watering crops and pasture](https://substack.com/redirect/a49f9baa-cfdd-4daf-bb3b-a0573e090910?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) but doesn't include watering people's yards, is [the largest use of water](https://substack.com/redirect/a49f9baa-cfdd-4daf-bb3b-a0573e090910?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) in the United States.
8
There's a whole [water science glossary](https://substack.com/redirect/0ce1990b-dd36-4b2e-a9e2-1ca566a821e9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) from the U.S. Geological Survey!
9
This [varies considerably based on where power comes from](https://substack.com/redirect/0dd26059-7953-43b3-9d93-674649934989?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). Wind, for instance, consumes very little water; coal and nuclear, on the other hand, consume substantial water.
10
Other [estimates on this vary](https://substack.com/redirect/8a77eedf-2505-4513-85e7-48a39850a912?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), in [some cases considerably](https://substack.com/redirect/62d80f3a-f73c-4bce-82dc-d491031f4ac2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). As I noted before, it's pretty shockingly difficult to get reliable, consistent estimates for water use. So I'm doing the best that I can, though other sources might have other estimates.
11
This is especially true for crop irrigation, where water use is _way_ higher in the spring and summer than in the fall or winter:
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/a49f9baa-cfdd-4daf-bb3b-a0573e090910?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Source: [U.S. Geological Survey](https://substack.com/redirect/a49f9baa-cfdd-4daf-bb3b-a0573e090910?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
This is intuitively obvious. But it's still surprising to see the full extent to which this is true.
12
It's worth noting that Google, as of 2021, was [between the fifth- and tenth-largest employer](https://substack.com/redirect/d614cfe7-6c82-4849-8ade-9ea1e68d9636?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) in Wasco County, Oregon, where The Dalles is the county seat. The data isn't more precise than that, but according to county records, Google employed between 101 and 250 people in the county.
13
Louisiana uses "parish" as its county-level designation, but it means the same thing.
14
And that was [before Meta's announced expansion](https://substack.com/redirect/195a54e3-3556-4b30-9acc-a6a677fbd8b6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg); I'm guessing it'll be even higher now.
15
I do think this opens the door for [Jevons paradox](https://substack.com/redirect/4090d894-2d13-4533-b844-40d594416d05?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), but:
* Demand for data centers is already growing so fast that I don't think systems that use water more efficiently will remove some major developmental bottleneck.
* Smart regulation will be critical in heading off this sort of overconsumption.

Every vote really does matter this year. Here’s how to cast yours early.

| | | | | | | [View this email in your browser](https://mailchi.mp/afc1d2cf98b5/the-next-56-days-matter-69641?e=561a28864e)
---

| | | | |
---
| |

Friends,

Early voting is not open across Wisconsin, and I ask you to make a plan to get your ballot in. We need you to bank your vote. I won't sugarcoat it. Control of Congress is at risk this year. The House majority could come down to a handful of seats and a few thousand votes, and Wisconsin is right in the middle of it. **Every vote really does matter.** It doesn't stop there. The races for Governor, Attorney General, and the State Legislature are all on the ballot, and each one will shape the future of Wisconsin for years to come. **Please vote the whole Republican ballot, top to bottom.** You can vote early in person at your local clerk's office or voting site now through Sunday, November 1. Hours and locations vary by community, so check yours at MyVote.wi.gov. It only takes a few minutes, and once your ballot is in, you're done. Remember to take your photo ID. When you go, I ask you to bring someone with you. Remind a friend, a neighbor, or a family member to vote too. That's how we win. We have just two weeks left.[ ](https://us.list-manage.com/w85JiOIS_yI?e=561a28864e&c2id=c7ba3a2bb578965816da09c04ea0f7a1)[**If you're able, a contribution of any amount today helps us reach more voters before Election Day.**](https://us.list-manage.com/OQ1uG_cDmo5?e=561a28864e&c2id=c7ba3a2bb578965816da09c04ea0f7a1)
Thank you for standing with me. Let's get it done! Scott Fitzgerald
P.S. Once you have voted, forward this email to a friend or family who hasn’t yet. That’s how we save Wisconsin and hold the House. [Please click here to chip in today!](https://us.list-manage.com/tGGV2QobgMU?e=561a28864e&c2id=c7ba3a2bb578965816da09c04ea0f7a1)

HELP US REACH EVERY VOTER
We have just **13 days** to get our message into every corner of PA-11 and make sure voters know they have a choice on November 3.
| | Reaching voters takes resources. Billboards, digital and traditional media advertising, mail, signs, and organizing across the district all cost money. **Your contribution today** will help us reach more voters and build the campaign we need to win!

---
**The Debate Is On!**
---
---
Thank you to everyone who publicly called on Congressman Smucker to debate Nancy. We’re excited to announce that he has agreed and the debate will take place Friday, October 23, from 4:00 – 5:30pm in Lancaster. The event will be hosted by the Lancaster Chamber and York County Economic Alliance. Tickets to attend sold out almost immediately, however, the organizers are working on options to livestream the event. We'll share these details later this week once they are finalized.

**Our Generation, Our Vote, Our Future:****A College Student’s Call to Young Voters**
As the election day gets closer, conversations matter more than ever. It can be tempting to stick with our in-groups or rely on hope that the election will magically go in our favor. But we must reach beyond that.
Ask yourself this question: Do you know any youth voters? If you have a child, sibling, friend, or friend of a friend aged 18-24, ask them what their voting plan is. Ask them about what matters to them, their worries, and the PA-11 they want to live in. Chances are they will bring up affordability; an issue Nancy Mannion is championing.
I’m a 22-year-old college student, which means I rely on mail-in ballots every election cycle. This November is no exception, as I cast my vote for Nancy from my one-bedroom apartment in Washington, D.C.
Living in D.C., I am ready to see Nancy on Capitol Hill fighting for an affordable PA-11, for my family in Lancaster County and for all of you.
My generation is constantly told that “we are the future” and that “it is up to us.” It’s exhausting to worry about what our future will look like, whether we’ll ever be able to buy a house or get by in a constantly changing world. If we are the future, then we need to do something about it.
This week, I encourage you to find a youth voter near you and make sure they have a plan. Whether they are home or will vote by mail, every ballot counts.
Nancy’s been putting in the work. Young voters need to as well. Start a conversation, make a plan, and know that we matter in this race.
_Contributed by Mia Ribich, PA-11 voter_

**Town Halls 12 and 13!****** This week, Nancy held her 12th and 13th public town halls of the year – Tuesday at Zoetropolis Cinema Stillhouse in Lancaster and Thursday at the New Freedom Community Center.

If you want to snuff out a radical political movement, you don't argue with the mob in the street... you take down the billionaires signing their checks.
That's what Trump is doing.
For years, the political left has enjoyed an endless stream of cash flowing from guilty billionaires, weaponized nonprofits, and bloated government agencies.
But that era is coming to a grinding halt. In addition to targeting street-level agitators, the Trump administration is actively dismantling the financial infrastructure that makes this radical organizing possible in the first place.
One such case, that nobody is talking about, is the absolute absurdity of James Cox "Fergie" Chambers Jr. If you want a poster child for the champagne socialist, Fergie is it. He's an heir to the massive Cox Enterprises fortune who cashed out his stake in 2023 for a cool $250 million. And what is he doing with that capitalist windfall? Funding communism.
Chambers isn't hiding this, by the way. He openly states, "I'm an American communist. My primary position in life is to extract as much of my family's hoarded wealth as possible and reappropriate it to revolutionary organizing." He's even called for building a "revolutionary communist party organized around Marxist-Leninist principles."
But the revolution has hit a major legal roadblock. Chambers is currently sitting in a jail cell in Ibiza. U.S. authorities have indicted him and are seeking his extradition from Spain over allegations of money laundering, riot-related offenses, and, crucially, transferring roughly €7 million connected to Hamas.

_**(Piece continues):**_
Just last week, Spain's National Court denied his request for release for the fourth time. Like all communists Chambers cries political prosecution, but the feds are following the money.
And Chambers's case isn't an isolated incident. We are witnessing a massive crackdown on the financial networks of the far-left.
Another example: Neville Roy Singham, the deep-pocketed financier behind radical outfits like The People's Forum. He is currently staring down a federal grand-jury investigation over potential foreign-agent violations. Then there's ActBlue, still tangled up in congressional investigations over fraud controls and alleged illegal foreign contributions. Reid Hoffman's American Future Republic? Under a DOJ investigation for potential money laundering tied to the E. Jean Carroll litigation. Even the Southern Poverty Law Center (SPLC) was federally indicted earlier this year on fraud and money-laundering charges.
The scrutiny isn't stopping at private bank accounts, either. Federal agents recently raided Rep. Ilhan Omar's home, seizing her phone as part of a sweeping immigration-fraud investigation. Meanwhile, the administration is heavily scrutinizing rampant childcare and program fraud in Minnesota, continuing prosecutions from the massive Feeding Our Future scheme.
And we can't forget the ultimate piggy bank: USAID. The administration exposed how USAID was funneling taxpayer dollars into left-wing programs that had zero to do with America's core interests. The result? They gutted it. By March 2026, thousands of grants were terminated, the workforce was slashed from roughly 13,600 down to a couple hundred, and the agency was effectively absorbed into the State Department.
Democratic critics are predictably crying foul, claiming federal law enforcement is being "weaponized." But to anyone who has watched these networks operate with impunity for the last decade, this doesn't look like weaponization. It looks like overdue accountability.
The radical left's financial infrastructure is finally being dragged into the light. It's about time.
This is, once again, another feather in Trump's cap to show the American people for the midterms. We are lied to, time and time again, and told that Trump hasn't delivered on his promises. We are told that he hasn't made meaningful long term change in the country. This is simply untrue, and all we have to do is follow the money to prove it.

**October 21, 2026**
Around our table, one story often retold is that of Moses, our Barred Rock rooster. He was named after the biblical Moses who encountered the burning bush. Hatched on our farm and raised by his mother hen alongside two other chicks, he grew into a stunning bird, but his beauty paled beside his character.
Whenever Moses found food in abundance, he would scratch, cluck, dance, and repeatedly pick up and drop morsels, calling the hens to gather. He kept the other roosters at bay as the hens ate their fill. Only when they were satisfied did Moses eat. And when he had finished, he allowed the other roosters their turn.
That was Moses, throughout his life, and we have never had another like him. His actions told his story, and his story remains at our table.
Long after a life ends, what we have done continues to tell others who we are.
**Pause. Breathe. Look Deeper.**
**Refuel.**
**Welcome to Sweet Ground.**

He was named after the biblical Moses who encountered the burning bush. Hatched on our farm and raised by his mother hen alongside two other chicks, he grew into a stunning bird, but his beauty paled beside his character. Whenever Moses found food in abundance, he would scratch, cluck, dance, and repeatedly pick up and drop morsels, calling the hens to gather. He kept the other roosters at bay as the hens ate their fill. Only when they were satisfied did Moses eat. And when he had finished, he allowed the other roosters their turn. That was Moses, throughout his life, and we have never had another like him. His actions told his story, and his story remains at our table. name: Roy Cooper
subject: You’ve been brought to my attention
body:
There’s something I need you to know, Peter
| [](https://act.roycooper.com/go/15912?refcode=email_fr_pros_jtk1723&source=&t=1&akid=4745%2E124072%2EHuUtiL) | | | | | | Peter, I’m not reaching out to everyone today. Just a select few, like you.
---
My team was going through our supporter records, and took particular notice of yours – because it showed that YOU are one of my most attentive grassroots supporters. You’ve been getting these emails for a while now, and we see you're keeping up with the latest on this election. I want you to know that _I know_ how engaged you’ve been with our campaign and how much I appreciate it.
**Today, I’m asking you to take the next step by** [**_making your first donation of $5_**](https://act.roycooper.com/go/15912?refcode=email_fr_pros_jtk1723&amount=5&t=9&akid=4745%2E124072%2EHuUtiL)**– here’s why:**
Republican super PACs have spent millions in North Carolina just to defeat me, and President Trump has personally intervened on behalf of his hand-picked MAGA candidate, Michael Whatley.
President Trump was even in North Carolina _today_ to spread lies about me and push support for Whatley. We need to respond fast – and the first step is reaching our $1 million rapid-response goal by midnight. [**_Will you please chip in $5 right now to help us get there in time? I’m not exaggerating when I say that the stakes couldn’t be higher:_**](https://act.roycooper.com/go/15912?refcode=email_fr_pros_jtk1723&amount=5&t=10&akid=4745%2E124072%2EHuUtiL)
See, North Carolina is the best chance Democrats have to flip one of the four seats we need to take back the Senate. **But if we lose here, we lose our shot at flipping the majority.**
The best way we can avoid the latter is by proving that North Carolina cannot be bought so easily.

Two polls show me **_tied_** w/ my MAGA opponent in a state Trump carried by 20 pts - a dead heat. 8% of voters don't know who I am but polling shows after they see our bio on TV ads, we LEAD by 9 points. We were told _the cavalry from DC was on its way to put up TV ads in this race_ like they’re doing in close races like ours across the nation. **We waited and we waited.** [](https://click.actionnetwork.org/ss/c/u001.iIBo0N5fSFzEFL40Tn-vtbMETCUYClkOrOh9-SNJfqu9_34IA0ihQL9SBkbAGz1bI952SqTZGgIGaigNitpp3-NhqCP3IHSyfoDG3eKKNIKZedjOVlcs9hfbMUZ7BazzSlnNlOkd9AgUTLYuC25zHNkMi9tOtiZOKnKg_vPu6qt_pHyn6wmyi6Q2RrOuIAETqostALX-sJ5ev6d7PO7QCUaNobB8dNw4bdF3YMXW2iOX_Cr5btNAESRq1a5oBdV_X2c1YKQ0LWEQZhFI9xKDVsK1EiiMB4gG723vWUyFIW8J73jQbRrAsQWzANvRRji7fb5Q02Oxjz6DkMa4M2VWOAnNrIXO-1mK3zsGd6wZzE3DWL1w0pwtlhV0VRLgO1wcoI4Uy1rrwY2jkYTU64cgwLQh5qIhAVk122gehxwSTv4/4v2/ogt-ti8bR5-_lDm-7y3neA/h1/h001.viCeYVjHEvL6CTX1-gI4L_db0llgx4kQiheIsNdt6Ag)

“We are highly trained agents who should be working child exploitation and trafficking cases, instead we are being used as pawns in our administration’s games.”
This confirms what most people already knew: The timing of the raid on Ilhan’s home was no accident.

But it doesn’t change the fact that the average price of a tank of gas is over $4, and a tank of diesel is almost $7. It doesn’t change the fact that millions of Americans are being kicked off their healthcare, while millions more struggle to afford it. It doesn’t change the fact that Trump and his buddies have been lining their own pockets while regular folks can’t afford groceries.
**Trump’s presidency is a failure, and on November 3rd the American people will send that message loud and clear.**

One town vanished for three years. Another changed the world. Discover the tiny places behind some of America's biggest moments.

| | |

Good Morning!**
****Some of the biggest moments in American history happened in places you've probably never heard of.** In this week's _Flyover Focus_ , we're taking you on a trip through [10 small towns that changed American history](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJysz01qwzAQQOHTSLsYzcg_8UKLQskuha4K3RjZHlkqshSscZzcvrT0CD3A9-B9XIerDTGk5c2uZNjlweVpL0Oio0Ripm1gT2W1MXI-UmFvefI2LTTbARW2J1AnhD8FcjaOCElLMtD12PQaGpTe6HNTowN0Ttupaanu8AzQt0AWzzSjDOanBgoBao1aVbpvJqKxbztUox5R1IrmwHmrvnJI7MnFZ77TVk15ldF45lsR-kXgReDlmXfeq5EEXvjx2r0n9Tg-D7mZ-XaEGENpO1GrZbUh_nr-h_W7we8AAAD__681b4M)--and the incredible stories behind them. [**➤ WATCH NOW: 10 Small Towns That Changed American History**](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJysz01qwzAQQOHTSLsYzcg_8UKLQskuha4K3RjZHlkqshSscZzcvrT0CD3A9-B9XIerDTGk5c2uZNjlweVpL0Oio0Ripm1gT2W1MXI-UmFvefI2LTTbARW2J1AnhD8FcjaOCElLMtD12PQaGpTe6HNTowN0Ttupaanu8AzQt0AWzzSjDOanBgoBao1aVbpvJqKxbztUox5R1IrmwHmrvnJI7MnFZ77TVk15ldF45lsR-kXgReDlmXfeq5EEXvjx2r0n9Tg-D7mZ-XaEGENpO1GrZbUh_nr-h_W7we8AAAD__681b4M) Forget Philadelphia, Boston, and Washington, D.C. Some of the events that shaped America happened in tiny towns with one stoplight, a single gas station, and a Main Street you could drive through in minutes. **Which American town officially didn't exist for three years while helping win World War II? Where did one of history's most famous inventions finally get off the ground? And which small town hosted a speech that helped define the Cold War?** From places where wars ended and legends were born to communities where groundbreaking technology took flight, these towns have some incredible stories to tell. And here's the part that might surprise you: **One of these towns could be in your own state. You may have even driven right through it without knowing what happened there.

clean_body: One town vanished for three years. Another changed the world. Discover the tiny places behind some of America's biggest moments. | | | Good Morning! Some of the biggest moments in American history happened in places you've probably never heard of. In this week's Flyover Focus , we're taking you on a trip through the incredible stories behind them. Forget Philadelphia, Boston, and Washington, D.C. Some of the events that shaped America happened in tiny towns with one stoplight, a single gas station, and a Main Street you could drive through in minutes. Which American town officially didn't exist for three years while helping win World War II? Where did one of history's most famous inventions finally get off the ground? And which small town hosted a speech that helped define the Cold War? From places where wars ended and legends were born to communities where groundbreaking technology took flight, these towns have some incredible stories to tell. And here's the part that might surprise you: One of these towns could be in your own state. You may have even driven right through it without knowing what happened there. Think you know your American history? Here's a challenge for you! Watch the countdown and see how many of these 10 towns you've heard of before. Can you name all 10? Or will a few surprise you? Once you've watched, drop your score in the YouTube comments or reply to this email and tell us how many you knew! ➤ Think you know your American history? See how many of these 10 towns you recognize! () If you enjoy this week's Flyover Focus - there's plenty more where that came from! Catch The Flyover Podcast for the news you need, seven days a week. () Thanks for cruising with us, The Flyover✈️ (Step One) The Flyover, LLC 1910 Thomes Ave. Cheyenne, WY 82001-3527 | ---|---

body:
Right now, our friends at Vote Forward are working to send as many letters as possible to voters in key races ahead of Election Day.
#
Hi there,
Right now, our friends at Vote Forward are working to send as many letters as possible to voters in key races ahead of Election Day.
**With just 3 days left to mail letters and ensure they arrive in time for the election, they need the Swing Left community’s support to finish strong!**
The Vote Forward letter-writing campaign that could use our help the most right now is **Voting History Letters** , which includes an individual’s personalized voting history (_whether_ they voted, not _who_ they voted for) alongside a personal message from a volunteer.
Past research has demonstrated that this strategy can make a real impact on voter turnout, which is why Vote Forward volunteers are currently working to send these letters to specific voters in Alaska, Georgia, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, Mississippi, North Carolina, Nebraska, New Hampshire, Ohio, and Texas who are less likely to show up to vote and are historically underrepresented.
[**Will you help make a difference in this year’s midterm elections by adopting voters and sending letters with Vote Forward today? You can click here to get started right now.**](https://act.swingleft.org/go/3195?t=1&akid=3235%2E1562180%2E9H3JxY)
**[Start Writing Now »](https://act.swingleft.org/go/3195?t=2&akid=3235%2E1562180%2E9H3JxY)**
Every letter you send is designed not only to boost voter turnout this year, but also helps the team at Vote Forward test and learn what works to shape the future of voter contact for years to come. And with over 200,000 voters still waiting to be adopted, there’s still time to put the power of a handwritten letter to work.
Thank you for everything you’re doing to make a difference this year!
— The Swing Left Team

**Since 2017, Swing Left has channeled the energy of grassroots volunteers and donors to elect Democrats, up and down the ballot, focusing on the most competitive races that can swing the national balance of power.** Right now, Swing Left is investing in grassroots organizing in key swing districts and initiatives across the country to flip the House and win the Senate and critical states in 2026. [**If you’d like to help support our work, you can make a donation using this link.**](https://secure.actblue.com/donate/em_ms_sl_footer?refcode=em20261021-2&t=3&refcode2=3235_1562180_9H3JxY&akid=3235%2E1562180%2E9H3JxY)

$26 billion.

for Michigan families, it’s imposing unfair, unsustainable choices in our

Dear Friend, this is your only warning. What I'm about to share with you is emotional \- PREPARE YOURSELF. ** The Rose Garden is almost sacred at night. When the cameras are gone and the noise of the day finally fades, it stops being a backdrop for press conferences and power plays. It becomes what it was always meant to be: a quiet, living garden right beside the White House. And last evening, in what could be my final 4 weeks as President, I took some time to reflect on the last 10 years we have shared as I strolled alongside the rose bushes. ****** Your faith in me still humbles me more than I can put into words. From the highest of highs to the lowest of lows, I have always been able to count on your support. From an unproven, underdog political candidate to the leader of our nation's GREATEST movement in history, you have always stood by my side. Even when it would have been easier to write me off. For the past decade, the Radical Left has done everything in their power in an attempt to destroy the MAGA coalition. They came for me, my family, friends, and above all: my supporters. People like you, Friend. When the chips were down, you stared evil straight in the face and never flinched. You put your career, family, and even LIFE on the line to continue supporting me, and I will never be able to thank you enough. Every single day I wake up, I pray and thank God for his blessing of being able to be your President. And every night I go to sleep, I pray for the opportunity to spend one more day fighting to make America Great Again. And in the Rose Garden late last evening, I made one final prayer before leaving: That my supporters will keep their trust in me one final time and help see the rest of my mission through. Last night, President Trump held a rally in North Carolina in support of my GOP opponent, Michael Whatley.
He told that crowd a lot of lies - about me, my record and the grassroots movement we're building.
And while visiting Hendersonville this week, JD Vance embarrassed himself _again_ when he implied "Raleigh-Durham" was the name of our capital city - you can tell he doesn't really leave the airport the few times he's been in NC!!
Now, a Trump-aligned super PAC is throwing a multimillion dollar lifeline Whatley's way in a last-ditch effort to buy his way into this seat.
I know I'm getting tired of this, and I'm sure you are, too, but we can't let up now.
Thanks to grassroots supporters like you, we've had the resources to fight back against the false attacks I've had to face thus far in the race. **[For that, I'm so grateful - but we're still falling behind on the $1 million rapid-response goal my team and I set.](https://substack.com/redirect/6f42d619-fe89-4899-aef4-c0886f04989d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**

The GOP has poured tens of millions into this race to defeat me - because if we fail to flip North Carolina from red to blue, Democrats will lose our chance at taking back the Senate.
With North Carolinians already casting their ballots, we urgently need to break through all of Trump's noise and reach voters with the truth. That's why it's essential that we get back on track ASAP, so I'm personally asking:
**[Will you chip in $5 or more now to help me push back against President Trump's lies, win in North Carolina and flip the Senate for the people?](https://substack.com/redirect/6f42d619-fe89-4899-aef4-c0886f04989d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**

Thank you. I really appreciate it.

Vivek Ramaswamy's campaign has put out an ad featuring Amy Acton's estranged mother attacking her own daughter. I think it pushes the boundaries of what we should accept in American politics.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/6f13f676-4ad3-4d25-bf76-eee6f5b2ce47?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
A mother appearing in a campaign ad to tell people not to vote for her child would be shocking enough. But understanding the backstory makes this much worse.
Acton has described a childhood marked by poverty, homelessness, and sexual abuse by her stepfather. Court records document the charges against him and the removal of Acton and her brother from their mother's custody.
Her brother, Philip Stearns, has publicly supported her account. In his statement condemning the ad, he said their mother stayed married to the man who abused Amy until he died.
This is a family estrangement stretching back decades. Ramaswamy's campaign decided to turn it into an attack ad.
That crosses a line I would hope Republicans and Democrats alike could recognize. But I do not see this slowing down. I see the boundaries getting pushed further, the behavior getting rewarded, and the next campaign learning that it can go even lower.
At what point are we living in _Idiocracy_ , if we are not already there?
* * *
## Trump Changed What a Debate Could Be
Shane Gillis has a stand-up bit about Trump's effect on presidential debates. It is funny because you can recognize exactly what he is talking about.
Other candidates would show up prepared to explain their positions and defend their records. Trump could interrupt, insult somebody's appearance, give them a nickname, and pull the entire conversation onto his terms.
We watched personal humiliation become part of the performance.
The 2015-2016 campaign brought attacks on opponents' looks, spouses, and family members. Ted Cruz's wife became material for a public insult. An unsupported story about Cruz's father and Lee Harvey Oswald became part of the political conversation.
And Trump kept going.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/e2399824-958b-4dbf-a759-7a1f058a551e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Funny enough, I watched _[Bombshell](https://substack.com/redirect/5dbead80-54c8-4552-804e-d58a9a6676ff?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_ yesterday. It brought me back to Megyn Kelly questioning Trump during that first Republican debate about how he talked about women, and the backlash she faced afterward.
That should have been a straightforward accountability question. Instead, the confrontation itself became another spectacle.
What might once have been treated as evidence that a candidate could not conduct himself appropriately became something supporters celebrated. He was fighting. He was unfiltered. He was saying what other people supposedly would not.
The question became less about whether the behavior was acceptable and more about whether the performance worked.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/9e1fb103-f22a-41f8-876e-64284ce0c8e4?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Bombshell Movie
* * *
## The Smaller Boundaries Shift, Too
This is not only about Trump, and it is not only about the most serious examples.
We have changed expectations about how elected officials talk, dress, conduct themselves, and treat other people. Those changes do not all carry the same moral weight, but they contribute to a broader question about what we expect from public office.
Take John Fetterman's shorts and hoodie. The Senate briefly relaxed its dress expectations in 2023 before adopting a bipartisan requirement for business attire on the floor.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/677c6dde-f465-46ea-b881-375a3794859c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Put On A Damn Suit John Fetterman
Obviously, wearing shorts is not comparable to exploiting somebody's childhood abuse. But it is still an argument about institutional standards. Does conventions matter?
Profanity is another example. Personally, I do not have a problem with profanity. You read this newsletter. You know that.
But its role in politics has changed. A public F-bomb can now be presented as proof that a politician is passionate, authentic, or fed up just like you.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/71b6e7e7-15e1-40c4-abd2-7d632d501d4c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
A word that might once have produced days of demands for an apology can become the clip somebody shares because they love how "real" the politician sounds.
I am not arguing that every old convention deserves to survive. I am asking whether we are consciously deciding which standards to change, or just accepting whatever gets the biggest reaction.
* * *
## We Cannot Excuse It Because We Like the Person
Look at Jasmine Crockett's confrontation with Marjorie Taylor Greene.
Greene insulted Crockett's appearance. Crockett responded with the "bleach-blonde, bad-built, butch body" line. The exchange went viral, and Crockett announced merchandise built around it to benefit House Democrats.
Yes, Greene started the personal attack. I understand why people enjoyed seeing her get it back.
But if we are talking about the standards of Congress, we should also acknowledge what happened afterward. A congressional hearing produced a personal insult, the insult became entertainment, and the entertainment became a fundraising opportunity.
That is an incentive.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/7de74244-d1c2-45c7-afc6-735c323a9b87?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
We cannot criticize the degradation of public office only when the person doing it belongs to the other party.
Then there was Greene displaying sexually explicit photographs of Hunter Biden during a congressional hearing. Whatever questions Congress wanted to investigate, putting those images in front of cameras was a choice about public humiliation.
Lauren Boebert was removed from a performance of _Beetlejuice_ after disruptive behavior. Video showed vaping and apparent intimate touching. She later apologized and went on to win election in a different congressional district in 2024.
The incident did not end her career. That does not prove voters liked the conduct. It does show it was not disqualifying.
The standards are becoming difficult to identify because the consequences are so inconsistent.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/ac7124b6-15bb-424d-a3fd-6b11cf31c2ce?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Lauren Boebert being removed from theater
* * *
## Even Disgrace Can Become a Business Opportunity
George Santos actually was expelled from Congress.
So accountability has not disappeared completely. But even there, look at what followed.
He turned his notoriety into personalized videos on Cameo. By January 2025, prosecutors said he had earned approximately $400,000 from those appearances.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/de5e469b-b0c2-49b1-85f9-3365c3bb8477?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Getting thrown out of Congress helped create an audience willing to pay for a message from him.
That is a different kind of consequence from disappearing from public life in disgrace.
It also gets to something larger. A scandal can cost somebody a position while still increasing their commercial value. Public embarrassment can create a new audience. The person becomes a character, and people pay to keep watching.
Once that happens, how much deterrent does embarrassment really provide?
* * *
## The Algorithm Does Not Need You to Approve
Social media has changed the incentives around all of this.
The recent movie _[The Social Reckoning](https://substack.com/redirect/f70c3a2b-f376-4135-9fb8-d348153ff04f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_ brings attention back to Facebook and the decisions behind what people see. The term I was trying to remember is **meaningful social interactions** , or MSI.
Facebook announced that shift in 2018. It was about prioritizing interactions between people, including conversations and sharing, rather than simply putting content in front of someone to consume.
It was not literally a system where only shares mattered, and I am not claiming those historical rules describe every platform's algorithm today.
But the broader problem is easy to recognize: Content can spread because people are furious about it.
You see an awful ad. You share it and say, "Can you believe this?"
Somebody else shares it because they think it is hilarious. Another person posts a response. A news outlet covers the backlash. A commentator makes a video about the news coverage.
Everybody has a different opinion. The ad keeps moving.
Your condemnation can help distribute the same material you want people to reject.
**And I am part of that. I am writing about the Acton ad. I am showing examples of the behavior I think has gone too far. Calling something out does not stop me from contributing to its exposure.**
A campaign does not need you to agree with its ad for the ad to dominate the conversation.

## AI Lets Campaigns Manufacture the Performance
Artificial intelligence adds another level.
We are moving beyond choosing an embarrassing photograph or cutting a real quote in a misleading way. Campaigns can now manufacture a recognizable person appearing to do something that never happened.
Ken Paxton's campaign used an AI-generated James Talarico in an ad involving a fictional Bible. It mixed actual remarks with missing context and a synthetic presentation.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/71165948-b3de-4439-9125-139069d06bac?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Think about that. Instead of showing you the candidate's actual appearance and explaining what is wrong with what he said, a campaign can construct its own version of him.
Through October 11, more than $137 million had reportedly been spent running 220 identified political ads containing AI-generated or AI-enhanced material.
That is spending to distribute those ads, not just the cost of making them.
We have already struggled to maintain standards when dealing with real footage. Now we are adding invented footage, artificial voices, and scenes created specifically to provoke a reaction.
The cost of producing more outrageous material is falling. The incentive to make it spread is still there.
* * *
## A Song About Somebody's Family Becomes the Ad
Look at the attack on Troy Jackson in Maine.
A Republican super PAC, Senate Leadership Fund, put out a song targeting his relationship with his partner, who is reportedly his second cousin. The relationship is legal.
The ad turns it into a sexual joke, with the chorus: "If he'll screw his own family, he'll screw yours, too."
Susan Collins's campaign called for the ad to be taken down. It is important to identify who actually made it rather than attribute it to her campaign.
But somebody still decided this was worth producing and distributing.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/c38e1ed4-d907-4691-89a8-3f7fb29d3139?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
It sounds like the kind of thing AI makes easier to churn out. Regardless of the production method, the decision to make somebody's family relationship into a catchy sexual insult was human.
And people like it. Some people find it funny. They share it.
The audience can reward the very thing we say we wish campaigns would stop doing.
* * *
## "Authentic" Can Mean Almost Anything Now
Drinking and campaigning offer another example of how perception can change.
Indiana local candidate Jaime West went viral after a televised forum. In a later interview with Piers Morgan, she acknowledged having three beers beforehand.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/a6cdc497-5f1e-40a5-84b3-779be78ec67f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Some people saw an embarrassing lack of judgment. Others saw somebody speaking plainly and refusing to act like a conventional politician.
I have also heard the claim that attacks portraying Amy Acton as drinking too much were pulled because they made her seem more relatable.
* * *
## My Tinfoil-Hat Theory About Political Scandal
Here is my own theory, and I am calling it a theory.
I increasingly wonder whether some controversies do less damage than we assume because the publicity itself becomes useful.
We should question the assumption that more exposure to something embarrassing automatically means less support.
Look at Max Miller's divorce controversy. His campaign has incorporated the family difficulties into its own advertising and accused opponents of exploiting them.
That is an attempt to take negative coverage and turn it into a narrative the campaign can use.
Whether it works is another question. But the strategy recognizes that attention can be reframed.
A voter might reject an allegation, dislike the people making it, or interpret the criticism as proof that their candidate is being targeted. Someone who was already committed may simply stay committed.
So the controversy spreads and name recognition goes through the roof!
I have experienced a version of this myself. After our election, Max Miller posted a photograph with my mother, who was at a Trump rally.
My mother is entitled to her political opinions. That is not the issue. What is shown was his decision to use her photograph to punctuate a public dig at me after he had already won. Would this have be acceptable 30 years ago?
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/a07b79c1-e4d7-43a1-a20a-7eec379d87d1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* * *
## And Now We Are Using Childhood Trauma
Which brings me back to Amy Acton.
Her mother's appearance in this ad is not a policy disagreement. It is an attempt to use a deeply painful family history to undermine her credibility.
The statement from Acton's brother describes what happened to them and says their mother remained married to the man who abused Amy.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/76eb1e9e-ede8-416d-861a-a7d95995ce7c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Knowing that history changes how you understand the ad. This is not simply a relative saying, "I disagree with her tax plan."
And after the backlash, Ramaswamy's campaign acknowledged producing it and announced plans to spend $4 million promoting it.
That is what makes this moment so disturbing to me. The criticism has not caused the campaign to step back. It is investing in getting the message in front of more people.
Maybe it believes the ad will persuade voters. **Maybe the controversy itself provides useful exposure.** We will not know the electoral result until people vote.
But I do not need an election result to decide that using this history in this way crosses a line.
If winning requires doing that, what exactly are you asking people to reward?
* * *
## When Is Enough Enough?
There are big and small examples here. Clothing, profanity, personal insults, sexual humiliation, synthetic depictions, and childhood abuse are different things.
But across them, I keep coming back to the same concern: We are losing the ability, or the willingness, to say that public office requires standards that apply even when breaking them benefits our side.
An insult becomes merchandise. A scandal becomes a paid appearance. A cruel ad becomes national news.
The next campaign sees the attention and decides how much further it can go.
I do not see that slowing down on its own. I worry it will accelerate as the tools get cheaper and the rewards for provoking people get larger.
So where is the line? Have we already crossed it? What would someone have to do for their own party, donors, supporters, or voters to say, "Enough"?
Do we still expect more from our representatives, campaigns, and news media than whatever produces the most clicks and reshares?
I want to hear what you think. Does this get worse, or can we stop rewarding it?

An unsupported story about Cruz's father and Lee Harvey Oswald became part of the political conversation. And Trump kept going. Funny enough, I watched yesterday. It brought me back to Megyn Kelly questioning Trump during that first Republican debate about how he talked about women, and the backlash she faced afterward. That should have been a straightforward accountability question. Instead, the confrontation itself became another spectacle. What might once have been treated as evidence that a candidate could not conduct himself appropriately became something supporters celebrated. He was fighting. He was unfiltered. He was saying what other people supposedly would not. The question became less about whether the behavior was acceptable and more about whether the performance worked. | | ---|---|--- Bombshell Movie The Smaller Boundaries Shift, Too This is not only about Trump, and it is not only about the most serious examples. We have changed expectations about how elected officials talk, dress, conduct themselves, and treat other people. Those changes do not all carry the same moral weight, but they contribute to a broader question about what we expect from public office. Take John Fetterman's shorts and hoodie. The Senate briefly relaxed its dress expectations in 2023 before adopting a bipartisan requirement for business attire on the floor. | | ---|---|--- Put On A Damn Suit John Fetterman Obviously, wearing shorts is not comparable to exploiting somebody's childhood abuse. But it is still an argument about institutional standards. Does conventions matter? Profanity is another example. Personally, I do not have a problem with profanity. You read this newsletter. You know that. But its role in politics has changed. A public F-bomb can now be presented as proof that a politician is passionate, authentic, or fed up just like you. A word that might once have produced days of demands for an apology can become the clip somebody shares because they love how "real" the politician sounds. I am not arguing that every old convention deserves to survive. I am asking whether we are consciously deciding which standards to change, or just accepting whatever gets the biggest reaction. We Cannot Excuse It Because We Like the Person Look at Jasmine Crockett's confrontation with Marjorie Taylor Greene. Greene insulted Crockett's appearance. Crockett responded with the "bleach-blonde, bad-built, butch body" line. The exchange went viral, and Crockett announced merchandise built around it to benefit House Democrats. Yes, Greene started the personal attack. I understand why people enjoyed seeing her get it back. But if we are talking about the standards of Congress, we should also acknowledge what happened afterward. A congressional hearing produced a personal insult, the insult became entertainment, and the entertainment became a fundraising opportunity. That is an incentive. We cannot criticize the degradation of public office only when the person doing it belongs to the other party. Then there was Greene displaying sexually explicit photographs of Hunter Biden during a congressional hearing. Whatever questions Congress wanted to investigate, putting those images in front of cameras was a choice about public humiliation. Lauren Boebert was removed from a performance of Beetlejuice after disruptive behavior. Video showed vaping and apparent intimate touching. She later apologized and went on to win election in a different congressional district in 2024. The incident did not end her career. That does not prove voters liked the conduct. It does show it was not disqualifying. The standards are becoming difficult to identify because the consequences are so inconsistent. | | ---|---|--- Lauren Boebert being removed from theater Even Disgrace Can Become a Business Opportunity George Santos actually was expelled from Congress. So accountability has not disappeared completely. But even there, look at what followed. He turned his notoriety into personalized videos on Cameo. By January 2025, prosecutors said he had earned approximately $400,000 from those appearances. | | ---|---|--- Getting thrown out of Congress helped create an audience willing to pay for a message from him. That is a different kind of consequence from disappearing from public life in disgrace. It also gets to something larger. A scandal can cost somebody a position while still increasing their commercial value. Public embarrassment can create a new audience. The person becomes a character, and people pay to keep watching. Once that happens, how much deterrent does embarrassment really provide? The Algorithm Does Not Need You to Approve Social media has changed the incentives around all of this. The recent movie brings attention back to Facebook and the decisions behind what people see. The term I was trying to remember is meaningful social interactions , or MSI. Facebook announced that shift in 2018. It was about prioritizing interactions between people, including conversations and sharing, rather than simply putting content in front of someone to consume. It was not literally a system where only shares mattered, and I am not claiming those historical rules describe every platform's algorithm today. But the broader problem is easy to recognize: Content can spread because people are furious about it. You see an awful ad. You share it and say, "Can you believe this?" Somebody else shares it because they think it is hilarious. Another person posts a response. A news outlet covers the backlash. A commentator makes a video about the news coverage. Everybody has a different opinion. The ad keeps moving. Your condemnation can help distribute the same material you want people to reject. And I am part of that. I am writing about the Acton ad. I am showing examples of the behavior I think has gone too far. Calling something out does not stop me from contributing to its exposure. A campaign does not need you to agree with its ad for the ad to dominate the conversation. | | | | ---|---|--- | Apr 9 | AI Lets Campaigns Manufacture the Performance Artificial intelligence adds another level. We are moving beyond choosing an embarrassing photograph or cutting a real quote in a misleading way. Campaigns can now manufacture a recognizable person appearing to do something that never happened. Ken Paxton's campaign used an AI-generated James Talarico in an ad involving a fictional Bible. It mixed actual remarks with missing context and a synthetic presentation. Think about that. Instead of showing you the candidate's actual appearance and explaining what is wrong with what he said, a campaign can construct its own version of him. Through October 11, more than $137 million had reportedly been spent running 220 identified political ads containing AI-generated or AI-enhanced material. That is spending to distribute those ads, not just the cost of making them. We have already struggled to maintain standards when dealing with real footage. Now we are adding invented footage, artificial voices, and scenes created specifically to provoke a reaction. The cost of producing more outrageous material is falling. The incentive to make it spread is still there. A Song About Somebody's Family Becomes the Ad Look at the attack on Troy Jackson in Maine. A Republican super PAC, Senate Leadership Fund, put out a song targeting his relationship with his partner, who is reportedly his second cousin. The relationship is legal. The ad turns it into a sexual joke, with the chorus: "If he'll screw his own family, he'll screw yours, too." Susan Collins's campaign called for the ad to be taken down. It is important to identify who actually made it rather than attribute it to her campaign. But somebody still decided this was worth producing and distributing. It sounds like the kind of thing AI makes easier to churn out. Regardless of the production method, the decision to make somebody's family relationship into a catchy sexual insult was human. And people like it. Some people find it funny. They share it. The audience can reward the very thing we say we wish campaigns would stop doing. "Authentic" Can Mean Almost Anything Now Drinking and campaigning offer another example of how perception can change. Indiana local candidate Jaime West went viral after a televised forum. In a later interview with Piers Morgan, she acknowledged having three beers beforehand. Some people saw an embarrassing lack of judgment. Others saw somebody speaking plainly and refusing to act like a conventional politician. I have also heard the claim that attacks portraying Amy Acton as drinking too much were pulled because they made her seem more relatable. My Tinfoil-Hat Theory About Political Scandal Here is my own theory, and I am calling it a theory. I increasingly wonder whether some controversies do less damage than we assume because the publicity itself becomes useful. We should question the assumption that more exposure to something embarrassing automatically means less support. Look at Max Miller's divorce controversy. His campaign has incorporated the family difficulties into its own advertising and accused opponents of exploiting them. That is an attempt to take negative coverage and turn it into a narrative the campaign can use. Whether it works is another question. But the strategy recognizes that attention can be reframed. A voter might reject an allegation, dislike the people making it, or interpret the criticism as proof that their candidate is being targeted. Someone who was already committed may simply stay committed. So the controversy spreads and name recognition goes through the roof! I have experienced a version of this myself. After our election, Max Miller posted a photograph with my mother, who was at a Trump rally. My mother is entitled to her political opinions. That is not the issue. What is shown was his decision to use her photograph to punctuate a public dig at me after he had already won. Would this have be acceptable 30 years ago? | | ---|---|--- And Now We Are Using Childhood Trauma Which brings me back to Amy Acton. Her mother's appearance in this ad is not a policy disagreement. It is an attempt to use a deeply painful family history to undermine her credibility. The statement from Acton's brother describes what happened to them and says their mother remained married to the man who abused Amy. | | ---|---|--- Knowing that history changes how you understand the ad. This is not simply a relative saying, "I disagree with her tax plan." And after the backlash, Ramaswamy's campaign acknowledged producing it and announced plans to spend $4 million promoting it. That is what makes this moment so disturbing to me. The criticism has not caused the campaign to step back. It is investing in getting the message in front of more people. Maybe it believes the ad will persuade voters. Maybe the controversy itself provides useful exposure. We will not know the electoral result until people vote. But I do not need an election result to decide that using this history in this way crosses a line. If winning requires doing that, what exactly are you asking people to reward? When Is Enough Enough? There are big and small examples here. Clothing, profanity, personal insults, sexual humiliation, synthetic depictions, and childhood abuse are different things. But across them, I keep coming back to the same concern: We are losing the ability, or the willingness, to say that public office requires standards that apply even when breaking them benefits our side. An insult becomes merchandise. A scandal becomes a paid appearance. A cruel ad becomes national news. The next campaign sees the attention and decides how much further it can go. I do not see that slowing down on its own. I worry it will accelerate as the tools get cheaper and the rewards for provoking people get larger. So where is the line? Have we already crossed it? What would someone have to do for their own party, donors, supporters, or voters to say, "Enough"? Do we still expect more from our representatives, campaigns, and news media than whatever produces the most clicks and reshares? I want to hear what you think. Does this get worse, or can we stop rewarding it? Stay Angry. Please think about donating or becoming a subscriber. | | ---|---|--- Join otherANGRY DEMOCRATS** by supporting Matt's work. _**\- NBC NEWS**_

This is just one example of the many nightmares tied to James Uthmeier's political stunt.
Alligator Alcatraz wasn't just an inhumane detention center, packed with overcrowded cages and substandard conditions. It was reckless with your tax dollars too.

Instead of listening to Coloradans, he's lining up right behind the corporate PACs funding his campaign. Now that we're on this list, Hurd's allies and the dark money behind them are going to spend heavily to keep this seat. I don't have that kind of money behind me. If you live in Texas, you have probably seen attack ad after attack ad about me. Let me be clear, these ads are simply not true, but unfortunately Abbott has the money to spread them far and wide.
**The only person who has raised property taxes in this race for governor is Greg Abbott.** Let me explain.
Greg Abbott took over Houston ISD with his own state-appointed board that then increased property taxes on the city of Houston.
